introduction: Start with the promise, estimate its demand, then define the requests and responses. These three draft stages help you explain a short-link service before choosing its data model or architecture. The remaining design stages are still being authored; this app does not create or redirect real short links.
invariant: An active short code resolves to exactly one destination and never silently changes ownership. Unknown or expired codes never redirect, including through a cache.

stages.title: Requirements and scope
stages.prompt: You are asked to design a service that creates short links and redirects readers. Write a short requirements brief: required operations, expiry and ownership rules, expected traffic, one measurable reliability or latency objective, abuse behavior, and non-goals. Which behavior must remain correct when a cache or database fails? State questions you would ask before choosing components.
stages.reference:
## Start with what the product must do

A short link is a stable name for a destination. Before drawing servers, agree on what creating and opening that name must mean.

### Required behavior

- Create a short code for an absolute HTTP(S) destination. Reject unsupported schemes, missing hosts, and destinations that point back into our own redirect service. This is a product validation policy; URI syntax alone does not establish that a destination is safe.
- Allow an optional expiry time. An active code identifies one destination. Creation must not silently replace someone else's code.
- Resolve a known, active code and redirect the reader. Unknown and expired codes must never redirect. In this workshop, choose 404 for both unknown and expired codes so the response does not distinguish their history. The API stage makes this policy explicit.
- Keep destination ownership stable. Do not reuse expired codes in this introductory design: an old shared link could otherwise lead to a new owner's destination.
- Define abuse controls for creation and opening links, and a takedown process. Automatic malicious-content scanning is outside this first scope. Creating a link does not require our server to fetch its destination.

### Correctness questions to resolve

An expiry check uses the link's expiry timestamp, including on a cache hit. At exactly the expiry time the link is expired. Cache TTL alone cannot promise this invariant if entries outlive the link.

A create request can time out after the server has stored a link. A retry must have a stated policy: a bounded client request key can return the original result, or the product can explicitly accept duplicate links. Do not assume a timeout proves nothing was created. The API stage below defines a bounded retry window and its limits.

### Assumptions to confirm with the interviewer or product owner

For this exercise, assume 1,000,000 daily users and 10 operations per user per day, of which 90% open links and 10% create them, with a peak factor of 5. These are illustrative assumptions, not measured demand. The Capacity module can calculate their effect.

Propose a redirect latency objective of p95 under 200 ms and 99.9% successful valid redirects over a 30-day window. Define the measurement boundary as the service's redirect response, excluding the destination page's load. Decide how planned maintenance and deliberate abuse rejection affect the success denominator. These targets are discussion inputs, not guarantees proved by our estimator or simulator. Availability for cached reads may differ from new writes during a store outage.

### Non-goals for the first design

Custom aliases, editable destinations, detailed click analytics, user accounts, multi-region writes, and a production shortening endpoint are outside this stage. Adding revocation later changes freshness requirements: a long cache TTL cannot promise immediate takedown.

### A tempting wrong answer

“Add Redis, a queue, and many service instances” names tools before agreeing what must remain correct. First define active-link ownership, expiry, expected operations, failure outcomes, and load. Introduce components only when an access pattern or bottleneck justifies them.

### Explain it aloud

**To a teammate:** “We create a stable code, and we redirect only while that code is active. Expiry must still be checked on cached reads. We need a retry policy for uncertain creates and explicit traffic and reliability assumptions before selecting infrastructure.”

**In an interview:** State create/resolve behavior, the ownership and expiry invariant, the read-heavy assumptions, measurable service objectives, and the first non-goals. Then ask which correctness or availability constraint is most important.

**Changed condition:** If links can be revoked immediately, what guarantee must cache invalidation provide? If click analytics becomes required, should recording a click delay a redirect? Name the new constraint before changing the design.

### Sources and scope

[RFC 9110, sections 15.4.3, 15.5.5 and 15.5.11](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.4.3) defines temporary redirects and the distinction between 404 and 410. The expired-code response above is a chosen product policy. [RFC 3986, sections 3 and 7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html#section-3) describes URI components and security considerations; accepting only HTTP(S) is our scoped design choice. Neither standard mandates this workshop's traffic, availability, ownership, or retry assumptions.

rubric.prompt: I named create and resolve behavior, plus unknown and expired-link outcomes.
I protected one-code/one-owner and expiry correctness, including cached reads and uncertain creates.
I stated traffic assumptions and a measurable objective with a clear observation boundary.
I stated abuse policy and non-goals, then named a condition that would change the design.

experimentLinks.instruction: Select the Interview baseline preset in Calculator. Compare peak factor 5 with 10; note which rates change and which daily totals stay fixed.

stages.title: Traffic and storage estimates
stages.prompt: Using 1,000,000 daily users, 10 operations per user per day, 90% reads and peak factor 5, estimate average/peak demand and daily new links. With 1 kB per new record, 365 days and three copies, estimate raw/replicated data. State what the estimate omits. Predict separately what changes if peak factor becomes 10, reads become 99%, or record size becomes 5 kB. Explain why these numbers cannot select server counts or prove a latency objective.
stages.reference:
## Count the work before choosing machines

An estimate turns product assumptions into quantities you can question. Use the Capacity module's **Interview baseline** preset; its Java calculator supplies the numbers below. They are illustrative assumptions, not measured traffic.

### Write down the inputs

- 1,000,000 daily users × 10 operations each; 90% open links and 10% create them.
- Peak factor 5; every create adds one 1 kB record; retain 365 days of raw records with three copies.
- For comparison with the existing calculator, assume a 2 kB average response, 200 ms mean total time and 30% planning headroom.
- Decimal units: 1 kB = 1,000 bytes; 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. A redirect response may be much smaller than 2 kB. Measure the create/redirect response mix before using that generic payload assumption in a real design.

### Carry the units through the arithmetic

- Daily operations: 1,000,000 × 10 = **10,000,000 requests/day**.
- Average demand: 10,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = **115.74 requests/s**.
- Busy-period demand: 115.7407 × 5 = **578.70 requests/s**.
- At that peak: 578.7037 × 0.9 = **520.83 reads/s**; × 0.1 = **57.87 writes/s**.
- New links: 10,000,000 × 0.1 = **1,000,000 writes/day**.
- New raw data: 1,000,000 × 1,000 bytes = **1 GB/day**. Retention: 1 × 365 = **365 GB raw**; three copies: 365 × 3 = **1,095 GB**.
- Response payload: 10,000,000 × 2,000 bytes = **20 GB/day**. At peak: 578.7037 × 2,000 × 8 ÷ 1,000,000 = **9.26 Mb/s**.
- Mean requests in the system: 578.7037/s × 0.2 s = **115.74 requests**, about 116. Time includes queueing and dependencies; this is not 116 CPU workers.
- A selected 30% margin gives 578.7037 × 1.3 = **752.31 requests/s** as a planning target. It does not prove that a fleet can sustain that load.

Displayed values are rounded after calculation. The 200 ms mean is an independent illustrative input, not a deduction from the Requirements stage's p95 objective. A mean does not establish a percentile or a burst bound.

### Change one assumption at a time

Reset **Interview baseline** before each change, then calculate again.

1. **Peak factor 10:** peak becomes **1,157.41 requests/s**, including **1,041.67 reads/s** and **115.74 writes/s**; peak response payload becomes **18.52 Mb/s**. Daily requests, daily writes and **365 GB raw** stay fixed because only the traffic concentration changed.
2. **Read percentage 99:** keep peak factor 5. Peak becomes **572.92 reads/s** and **5.79 writes/s**; creates fall to **100,000 writes/day**, so raw retained records fall to **36.5 GB**, or **109.5 GB** with three copies. Total request rate and response payload remain fixed under the unchanged response-size assumption. This depends on fewer creates, not simply on adding a cache.
3. **Record size 5 kB:** restore 90% reads. Raw retained data becomes **1,825 GB**, or **5,475 GB** with three copies. Requests/s and **9.26 Mb/s** response payload stay fixed because record size and response size are separate inputs.

### What this estimate cannot promise

Indexes, logs, backups, metadata, compression and operational reserve are excluded. A permanent code-reservation registry may grow after link records expire because our design never reuses an old code. The 24-hour create-retry records in the API stage also consume storage. Include those separately; 365-day raw link retention is not the whole long-term footprint.

Uniform request rates hide hot links and bursts. A cache may reduce store reads but does not change how many readers arrive at the service. Neither this worksheet nor the Request Flow simulator measures production instance capacity. Benchmark the chosen design with realistic workloads and failure cases, then inspect queue time, store latency and saturation.

### Correct a tempting wrong explanation

“Only 57.87 writes/s means any database is enough” skips record size, indexes, durability, hot partitions and degraded operation. Estimate the access pattern, then measure whether the chosen store meets the stated latency and correctness constraints.

**To a teammate:** “The baseline implies about 579 peak operations/s and 365 GB of raw records per year. Peak concentration changes rate, while the create fraction and record size change growth. We still need overhead, skew and failure measurements before choosing capacity.”

**In an interview:** State the assumptions; derive daily, average and peak work; separate reads from new records; explain decimal units and exclusions; change one assumption and defend which output moves. If retries increase arrivals without creating new records, model request demand separately from unique writes.

### Sources and scope

[Little's original paper, public abstract](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/opre.9.3.383) supports the average relationship under its stationarity and finite-mean conditions; it does not promise a worker count. [AWS load-testing guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/perf_process_culture_load_test.html) supports checking complete workloads against defined objectives. Our workload values and arithmetic are workshop assumptions verified against this app's Java estimator.

rubric.prompt: I carried requests/day, requests/s, kB and decimal GB through visible arithmetic.
I separated total traffic, read/create rates, new records, retained data and copies.
I changed peak, read percentage and record size independently and explained unchanged outputs.
I explained overhead, non-reuse/retry metadata, skew and why mean concurrency cannot prove worker or p95 capacity.

experimentLinks.label: Calculate and challenge the baseline
experimentLinks.instruction: In Calculator, select Interview baseline and calculate. Reset it before separately changing peak factor to 10, read percentage to 99, or record size to 5 kB. Compare rates, storage and response payload.

experimentLinks.label: Compare a daily average with a burst
experimentLinks.instruction: In Playground, select Finite queue overload and run. Inspect queued and rejected requests. Explain why mean concurrency from Calculator does not establish burst capacity.

stages.title: Create and redirect APIs
stages.prompt: Specify conceptual POST /links and GET /{code} requests, successful responses and errors. Walk through a create timeout after commit, a same-key retry with changed input, and a read at exactly the link expiry. Explain redirect caching and how you avoid leaking whether a code used to exist. State the retry window, authorization and abuse assumptions. These are proposed contracts, not endpoints implemented by this learning app.
stages.reference:
## Make each request's promise explicit

A contract tells a caller what success, failure and an uncertain result mean. These examples describe the service we are designing. The learning app only serves workshop content and simulations; it implements no shortening endpoints.

### Create one link

Use **POST /links** with JSON fields `destination` and optional `expiresAt`. Require an `Idempotency-Key` for retry protection. The name and behavior of this header are our product contract, not a guarantee provided by HTTP.

```http
POST /links
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: create-7

{"destination":"https://example.com/guide","expiresAt":"2026-11-01T00:00:00.000Z"}
```

After durable creation, respond **201 Created**, `Location: https://s.example/aB7x`, and `Cache-Control: no-store`:

```json
{"code":"aB7x","shortUrl":"https://s.example/aB7x","expiresAt":"2026-11-01T00:00:00.000Z"}
```

Our illustrative limits are an 8 KiB request body, a destination up to 2,048 characters, a 1–64 character ASCII request key matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` (no whitespace or control characters), and an optional UTC expiry after the current time and no more than 365 days ahead. Parse and validate the URL; accept only absolute HTTP(S) URLs with a host. Reject credentials in the URL, control characters and our own redirect-service origins to limit loops and header misuse. Do not fetch a destination during creation. A valid URL can still be malicious; validation is not a safety certificate.

For creation, assume an authorized API client credential supplies a stable caller namespace. Account management is outside this workshop. A public anonymous-create product would need a new caller/retry identity and abuse policy; an arbitrary caller-supplied namespace is not authorization. The public resolve operation needs no creator credential. Rate limits, quotas and a protected takedown workflow remain design requirements, not features implemented here.

### A timeout does not tell you whether creation committed

Define a **24-hour replay window** from successful creation. Store the caller namespace, key, parsed create fields, resulting code and original response together with the link creation, atomically. Authenticate the caller, parse and bound the fields, then look up the retained caller/key and compare the accepted fields, including expiry. A retained identical replay returns its recorded result before applying new-create validation such as requiring a future expiry. Only a new create must pass that future-expiry check. Different JSON whitespace is not a different create. Concurrent requests for the same namespace/key must not produce two links.

- **Same key, same create fields, within the window:** return the original 201 status, body and Location; do not create a second code. Replaying a response is not a new creation.
- **Same key, different accepted fields, within the window:** return **409 Conflict** with `request_key_conflict`; leave the first link unchanged.
- **The first request committed but its response was lost:** repeat the same key and fields within the window to obtain its recorded result. If the link has expired or been taken down since creation, the replay still describes the original creation; opening the code returns 404.
- **The first attempt is still in progress:** coalesce or wait within a bounded request deadline; if that deadline expires, return 503 `create_in_progress` and a bounded Retry-After. Retry with the same key rather than racing a new one.
- **The replay window has ended:** the key may be accepted as a new create. An old timeout is still ambiguous; a new key or expired key can produce a duplicate link. Longer deduplication needs a different retention/reconciliation contract.

For example, `create-7` commits at 10:00 but the caller times out. Repeating it at 10:01 returns `aB7x`. Changing its destination at 10:02 returns 409. At 10:00 the next day, the 24-hour window has ended and replay is no longer promised. The replay deadline belongs to the request record; it is separate from the short link's lifetime.

The implementation of atomic storage, durable retry records and concurrency control belongs in later Data and Flow stages. A separate best-effort cache of request keys would leave a crash window and cannot support the promise above.

### Open one active code

Use **GET /{code}**. First resolve the mapping and check expiry and takedown state, including when reading an application cache. At `now >= expiresAt`, do not redirect. For an active link, the chosen response is:

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://example.com/guide
Cache-Control: no-store
```

The Location is the destination here; in the creation response it identifies the created short link. Send no success redirect when a mapping's current eligibility cannot be established.

Choose `Cache-Control: no-store` for redirect and error responses so conforming HTTP caches do not reuse them instead of checking eligibility. **302 alone does not prevent caching.** This directive controls HTTP response caching; it does not invalidate our internal mapping cache or guarantee behavior by a hostile client. Immediate takedown still requires an authoritative eligibility check or a design that synchronizes revocation with cached copies. If that cannot be ensured during an outage, fail the read rather than claim immediate revocation.

### Make errors useful without revealing history

Return a bounded JSON error with `code`, a clear `message` and a request ID; omit stack traces, destination credentials and sensitive link metadata.

- **400:** malformed JSON, invalid destination, expiry outside the chosen limits or missing/invalid request key. A corrected request needs a new key if it changes a previously accepted create.
- **401/403:** missing/invalid create credentials or a disallowed create operation, under the assumed caller policy.
- **404:** unknown, expired or taken-down code, with the same outward response and no Location. This chosen privacy policy does not claim every implementation must use 404.
- **409:** conflicting reuse of a retained create key; return enough information to explain the conflict without exposing another caller's result.
- **429:** deliberate quota/rate rejection; define applicable limits and whether to include Retry-After. The exact enforcement policy belongs in the later abuse design.
- **503:** unavailable dependencies or a pending-create deadline; use Retry-After only when a useful retry delay is known. A create timeout/503 must not imply that nothing was stored.

### Change the requirement and revise the contract

If callers require replay for a week, retain request records for a week and budget their volume; link expiry and key expiry remain independent. If the product permits CDN redirect caching, define bounded freshness and takedown delay before changing no-store. A permanent cached redirect cannot satisfy immediate revocation merely because the database has been updated.

**Wrong explanation:** “POST is safe to retry because the server chose a unique code.” A unique code prevents one kind of collision; it does not stop two retries from creating two different codes. Only the stated caller/key/payload retention and atomicity contract addresses that duplicate effect within its window.

**To a teammate:** “Create returns one recorded result for a retained caller key. Resolve returns a temporary redirect only while the code is eligible, and HTTP responses are not stored. Internal cache freshness, revoked links and uncertain writes still need explicit failure handling.”

**In an interview:** Show create and resolve success, then trace one lost response and one expired read. Explain key scope and lifetime, 409 on changed fields, 404 privacy and why HTTP no-store differs from application-cache correctness. Defend the response behavior before choosing storage.

### Sources and product choices

[RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.3.2) defines 201, Location, 302 and the relevant error meanings; sections 9.2.2, 10.2.2, 10.2.3 and 15 explain method/retry and status semantics. [RFC 9111 section 5.2.2.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-5.2.2.5) defines the response no-store directive. [RFC 6585 section 4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6585#section-4) defines 429 and optional Retry-After. [RFC 3986 sections 3 and 7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html#section-3) cover URI components and security considerations. Our URL limits, 24-hour replay policy, credential assumption and expiry/privacy choices are explicitly chosen design rules; these standards do not implement them for us.

rubric.prompt: I described create 201 and resolve 302 with the correct meaning of each Location.
I scoped request keys, compared accepted fields, bounded replay to 24 hours and explained concurrent/uncertain creates.
I rejected unknown/expired/revoked codes at the eligibility boundary and distinguished HTTP no-store from internal cache freshness.
I explained validation, caller/abuse controls, 404 privacy, 409 conflict and honest 503 outcomes.

experimentLinks.label: Inspect why a cached mapping can be stale
experimentLinks.instruction: In Playground, run baseline, then inspect the origin update and later stale hit. Explain why Cache-Control: no-store on an HTTP redirect cannot fix internal cache eligibility checks.

experimentLinks.label: Choose an abuse failure policy
experimentLinks.instruction: In Playground, compare Counter backend outage with fail-open and fail-closed. Explain separate create and public-redirect priorities; this module does not implement request-key deduplication.
